title: Common Use Cases Across Domains
description: Where Python, Java, and C are each typically the strongest fit, across web, mobile, systems, data science, and more.
objectives: Identify typical strong-fit domains for each language
Understand why each language suits its typical domains

content.heading: Python
content.body: Data science and machine learning (NumPy, pandas, PyTorch, scikit-learn — a dominant ecosystem in this space), scripting and automation (quick, readable one-off or recurring tasks), web backends (Django, Flask, FastAPI), and education (its readability makes it a common first teaching language). Less common for mobile apps, low-level embedded work, or situations demanding the absolute lowest possible latency/overhead.

content.heading: Java
content.body: Enterprise backend systems (a long-standing, deeply established ecosystem — Spring and similar frameworks), Android app development (Java, alongside Kotlin, is a primary Android language), and large-scale distributed systems where portability, tooling maturity, and long-term maintainability across large teams matter greatly. Less common for systems/embedded programming or data science's numerical-computing core (though it has a presence in big-data tooling like Hadoop/Spark's JVM-based ecosystem).

content.heading: C
content.body: Operating system kernels and low-level systems programming (Linux, Windows, and most other major OS kernels are written substantially in C), embedded systems and firmware (where resource constraints and hardware-level control are paramount), device drivers, and performance-critical libraries that other, higher-level languages (including Python's own CPython interpreter, and many of Python's fast numerical libraries) are themselves implemented in or interface with. Less common for typical web/enterprise application development, where its lack of built-in safety and higher development cost outweigh its performance benefits for most such applications.

content.heading: Key Differences
content.body: The three languages occupy largely complementary, only lightly-overlapping niches rather than being direct competitors for most projects: C for systems/embedded/performance-critical foundations, Java for large-scale portable enterprise/Android applications, Python for data science, scripting, and rapid application development. It's also common (and often ideal) for a single system to combine them — a Python data pipeline calling into C-backed numerical libraries, for instance.

content.heading: When It Matters
content.body: Choosing a language for a new project should weigh the target domain's typical needs (raw performance vs. developer productivity vs. portability vs. ecosystem maturity for that specific kind of work) rather than a generic 'which language is best' framing.

keyPoints: Python dominates data science/ML, scripting, and is common for web backends and education
Java dominates enterprise backends and Android development, and large, portable, long-lived systems
C dominates operating systems, embedded/firmware, device drivers, and performance-critical foundational libraries
